a: One row of related data about a single thing
A single piece of data, such as a name
The data type given to a field
tasks.fb: One packet of seed, one record. The pieces inside it are the fields.

tasks.q: The library stores Name, Family and PacketsLeft about each packet. What is Family?
tasks.fb: A field is one named piece of data; the record is the whole row it sits in.

tasks.q: A field called Organic stores only True or False. What data type is it?
tasks.fb: A Boolean has only two possible values, so it is the smallest and safest choice here.

tasks.q: Why is every field given a data type?
a: So only sensible data of the right kind can be stored in it
So the records can be put into alphabetical order
So the table needs fewer fields
So the table can be printed
tasks.fb: The data type is a rule: text cannot be typed into an integer field.

tasks.q: What does  SELECT * FROM Seeds;  return?
a: Every field of every record in the Seeds table
Only the first record in the Seeds table
Only the fields whose names begin with S
The number of records in the Seeds table
tasks.fb: The star is a shorthand for all the fields, and with no WHERE nothing is filtered out.

tasks.q: What job does FROM do in a query?
a: It names the table the data is taken from
It lists the fields to return
It sets a condition the records must meet
It puts the results into order
tasks.fb: SELECT chooses the columns, FROM chooses the table and WHERE chooses the rows.

tasks.q: Using the Seeds table, which records does  WHERE PacketsLeft < 5  return?
tasks.fb: Runner Bean has 3 packets and Basil has 0, and both of those are below 5.

tasks.q: How is a piece of text written inside a WHERE condition?
a: With no punctuation at all, such as Legume
Inside a pair of hashes, such as #Legume#
tasks.fb: The quotes tell the database it is a value to compare, not the name of a field.

tasks.q: Using the Seeds table, which seeds does  WHERE Family = 'Legume' AND PacketsLeft > 5  return?
tasks.fb: Both legumes pass the first test, but Runner Bean has only 3 packets, so AND rules it out.

tasks.q: Which operator returns a record when at least one of two conditions is True?
tasks.fb: AND needs both sides to be True; OR needs only one of them.

tasks.q: What does the % wildcard stand for in a LIKE pattern?
a: Any number of characters, including none
tasks.fb: The underscore is the one that stands for exactly one character.

tasks.q: Using the Seeds table, which names does  WHERE Name LIKE 'S%'  return?
a: Every name that contains the letter s
tasks.fb: The pattern anchors the S to the start, so Radish is not returned even though it contains an s.

tasks.q: Match each WHERE line to the records it returns.
tasks.fb: Take one record at a time and ask whether the condition is True for it. If it is, the record is returned.

tasks.q: Which query would find every seed whose name ends in the letter n?
a: SELECT Name FROM Seeds WHERE Name LIKE '%n';
SELECT Name FROM Seeds WHERE Name LIKE 'n%';
SELECT Name FROM Seeds WHERE Name = 'n';
SELECT Name FROM Seeds WHERE Name LIKE '_n';
tasks.fb: Put the % before the letter and the pattern means anything, then n at the very end.

tasks.q: Build a query that lists the name and family of every legume with more than five packets left. Tap the parts in the right order.
tasks.fb: SELECT says which columns you want, FROM says which table they are in, and WHERE narrows it to the rows you want. Extra conditions join on with AND after the first WHERE, not as a second WHERE.

info.title: Why not one big list
info.text: A table of records keeps related data together, so one row can be added, changed or deleted without disturbing any other. Storing the same data as separate lists of names and separate lists of numbers makes it far too easy for the lists to drift out of step.

info.title: Primary keys
info.text: A field like SeedID that is different for every record is called a primary key. It matters because two packets could easily share a name, but a key is guaranteed to pick out exactly one record.

info.title: SQL is everywhere
info.text: The same SELECT, FROM and WHERE are used by almost every database in the world, from a school register to an airline booking system. Learning them once means you can query any of them.

info.title: The order the lines go in
info.text: SQL is read by the database in a fixed order: find the table named in FROM, keep only the records that satisfy WHERE, then return the fields listed in SELECT. Knowing that order explains why a query that returns nothing usually has a problem in its WHERE line.

info.title: One letter apart
info.text: Swapping AND for OR normally changes how many records come back, and OR almost always returns more. If a query gives too many results, an OR that should have been an AND is the first thing to check.

info.title: Searching as you type
info.text: When a website suggests results while you are still typing, it is usually running a LIKE query with a % on the end of whatever you have typed so far.

diagrams.title: How a query runs
diagrams.text: WHERE throws away the rows that fail the condition, and only then does SELECT pick the columns. Rows first, columns second.
